title: Intervals
intro: An interval is the distance between two pitches. It has two parts: a number (how many letter names it spans) and a quality (major, minor, perfect, augmented or diminished), fixed by the exact number of semitones.

blocks.text: Melodic and harmonic
Two notes played one after the other make a melodic interval; played together, a harmonic interval. The naming is the same either way.
Interval number

Count the letter names from the lower note to the upper, including both: C to E is C–D–E, a third; C to G is a fifth; C to the next C is an octave (an eighth). The number depends only on the letters, never on sharps or flats: C to E♭ and C♯ to E are both thirds.
Interval quality

Unisons, fourths, fifths and octaves are perfect intervals. Seconds, thirds, sixths and sevenths are major or minor. Make any of them one semitone larger and it becomes augmented; one semitone smaller and it becomes diminished (a minor interval made smaller is diminished; a perfect one, too).

items: Perfect unison P1: 0 semitones · minor second m2: 1 · major second M2: 2
minor third m3: 3 · major third M3: 4 · perfect fourth P4: 5
augmented fourth A4 / diminished fifth d5 (the tritone): 6
perfect fifth P5: 7 · minor sixth m6: 8 · major sixth M6: 9
minor seventh m7: 10 · major seventh M7: 11 · perfect octave P8: 12

blocks.text: A quick method: the intervals from the tonic of a major scale up to each scale note are all major or perfect (M2, M3, P4, P5, M6, M7, P8). So to name C–A, think 'A is the 6th note of C major, so C–A is a major sixth'. If the upper note is a semitone lower than the scale note, the interval is minor (or diminished, for perfect ones).

Switch the Tuning control to just and play the major third again: it is noticeably narrower and smoother than the equal-tempered one. The Tuning and Temperament (#/arts/music-theory/tuning) chapter explains why.
Enharmonic intervals

C–F♯ and C–G♭ are both six semitones, but C–F♯ is an augmented fourth (C to F is a fourth) and C–G♭ a diminished fifth (C to G is a fifth). Spelling matters because the two resolve differently: an augmented fourth tends to expand outward to a sixth, a diminished fifth to contract inward to a third.
Inversion

Inverting an interval moves the lower note up an octave (or the upper note down). The two intervals add up to an octave: the numbers add to 9 and the qualities swap major ↔ minor, augmented ↔ diminished, while perfect stays perfect. A major third C–E inverts to a minor sixth E–C (3 + 6 = 9); a perfect fifth inverts to a perfect fourth.
Compound intervals

Intervals wider than an octave are compound: a ninth is an octave plus a second, a tenth an octave plus a third. Subtract 7 to get the simple interval: an 11th is a compound 4th, a 13th a compound 6th. Jazz chord names use 9, 11 and 13 this way.
At the piano

Learn intervals as hand shapes. With the right hand, a fifth is thumb to little finger in a five-finger position (C to G); a third is thumb to middle finger; an octave is a full stretch from thumb to little finger. Recognising the sound matters as much: many musicians tie each interval to a song that starts with it ('Here Comes the Bride' for a rising fourth, the 'Star Wars' theme for a fifth, 'Somewhere over the Rainbow' for an octave).
Play along at the piano

items: Step 1. Put your right thumb on middle C. Count keys up (white and black) to find each interval: 3 keys up is E♭ (minor third), 4 is E (major third), 5 is F (perfect fourth), 7 is G (perfect fifth), 12 is the next C (octave).
Step 2. Play C with each of those notes, first one after the other, then together. Say the interval name as you play.
Step 3. Now start on D and find the same intervals by counting semitones: the major third above D is F♯ (4 semitones), the fifth is A.
Step 4. Learn the hand shapes: in a five-finger position (thumb on C), thumb-to-middle-finger is a third, thumb-to-little-finger a fifth.
Step 5. Press ▶ on each interval in the keyboard above in turn; Step ▶ then plays its two notes one at a time.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Name the intervals
blocks.text: Name each interval: D up to F; E♭ up to B♭; F up to B; G♯ up to F.
solution: D–F: a third (D E F) of 3 semitones = minor third.
E♭–B♭: a fifth of 7 semitones = perfect fifth.
F–B: a fourth of 6 semitones = augmented fourth (the tritone).
G♯–F: a seventh (G A B C D E F) of 9 semitones; a minor seventh is 10, so this is a diminished seventh.

blocks.title: Invert
blocks.text: Invert: M2, A4, m6, P5.
solution: Numbers sum to 9 and qualities swap: M2 → m7; A4 → d5; m6 → M3; P5 → P4.

blocks.title: Spell it
blocks.text: Spell the note a minor sixth above E, and a major sixth below F.
solution: A sixth above E is a C (E F G A B C). E to C is 8 semitones, which is a minor sixth already: C.
A sixth below F is an A (F E D C B A). A up to F is 8 semitones (minor); for a major sixth (9) the lower note must be a semitone lower: A♭.
